title: VPC control plane compact seller FAQ and fallback strategies
content:
Purpose:
A compact, conversation-ready FAQ + fallback-strategy cheat sheet for sellers, SEs, and GTM leaders when discussing Redwood Private (VPC / on-prem) with regulated buyers.

Context / framing (one-liner):
Customers who require regulatory controls want: a clear control plane boundary, auditable admin controls, predictable inference economics, and a low-risk pilot path. Our messaging should reduce perceived product risk and shorten procurement cycles by addressing the top 7 objections directly and offering concrete fallbacks.

Quick narrative to lead with (30–60s):
We run a private control plane that integrates with your cloud or on-prem infra so you keep operational control over keys, logs, and network egress. The control plane manages orchestration and model lifecycle metadata only — inference traffic and sensitive data stay inside your VPC. For auditors: we provide full audit trails, optional HSM/KMS integration, and an air-gapped installer for high-regulation environments.

Top buyer objections and suggested responses (short scripts):
1) "If we give you any control plane running it in our cloud, are we handing over data or keys?"
  - Script: "Short answer: No. The control plane stores orchestration metadata and model pointers only. You retain customer data and secrets in your KMS; we never persist raw payloads outside your VPC. If you prefer, we offer a private control plane that we deliver as a customer-controlled service (IP + installer) with an option for air-gapped install."
  - Tech note: call out KMS/HSM integrations, optional DB encryption at rest, and explicit retention window configs.

2) "How do you prove you didn’t tamper with model weights or inference code?"
  - Script: "We use signed artifacts and verifiable manifests for model packages; every change is recorded in an append-only audit log. For highest-assurance customers we support signed, pinned model releases and reproducible build artifacts you can validate in your pipeline."

3) "What happens if Redwood is unavailable — will our app fail?"
  - Script: "You can configure local fallback routing: if the managed control plane endpoint is unreachable, the runtime will continue serving pinned model binaries in your VPC. We also support a read-only local control plane mode so orchestration can continue for existing deployments."
  - Quick fact: Default local-fallback mode retains last-known model snapshot + KV cache warmup config.

4) "Is it possible to get compliance artifacts for SOC2, FedRAMP, or ISO?"
  - Script: "Yes — for customers on Dedicated/Private we provide an audit bundle and a compliance onboarding playbook. For regulated pilots, our security team will assign a checklist, and we can sign whatever NDA / data processing addendum is required before any exchange of data."

5) "Why not just self-host an open-source runtime?"
  - Script: "Open-source runtimes are a strong option for some teams but require substantial ops bandwidth to maintain kernel-level performance optimization, KV cache correctness, batching safety, and secure model updates. We deliver a hardened, performance-optimized runtime plus a control plane designed for safe rollouts, canarying, and emergency rollbacks — all integrated with observability and cost controls out of the box."

6) "How do you handle supply-chain risk for third-party models?"
  - Script: "We provide versioned model manifests, provenance metadata, and scanning hooks for known CVEs. Customers can opt to perform their own model validation or use our vetting pipeline. When customers require it, we also support allowlist-only model catalogs that block unapproved artifacts."

7) "What are the exit / migration guarantees if we stop using Redwood?"
  - Script: "You can export model artifacts, audit logs, and runtime configs. Our private deployments include an export tool to stream snapshots and manifests to your storage. We also provide a migration runbook for common target runtimes (OSS runtimes, cloud-managed endpoints)."

Competitive quick-comparison (talking points for SEs):
- Large cloud vendors: strength = integration with cloud native IAM and managed infra. weakness = limited choice of tuned open models, opaque unit economics for inference.
- LLM API providers: strength = turnkey API and model catalog. weakness = lack of private-control-plane options and limited on-prem tooling for audit-first buyers.
- Self-hosted OSS: strength = full control and zero vendor lock-in. weakness = heavy ops cost, no vendor SLA, and slow to adopt inference optimizations.

Positioning map snippet (for pitch):
- X axis: Time-to-value (fast -> slow).
- Y axis: Regulatory/Control Assurance (low -> high).
Redwood Private sits in the quadrant: moderate time-to-value, high regulatory assurance — because we combine a hardened runtime with a customer-controlled control plane and clear audit guarantees.

Fallback strategies and escalation ladder (practical runbook):
- Tier 0 (AE): Offer a security overview and schedule SE deep-dive. Provide compliance checklist and sample DPA.
- Tier 1 (SE): Walk infra diagram; demo KMS/HSM integration; provide log retention and audit export example.
- Tier 2 (Solutions Eng): Run a short proof-of-concept: deploy control plane in a sandbox VPC, pin a model, run a synthetic workload and capture latency/cost numbers.
- Tier 3 (Security SWAT): If third-party audit requested: hand off to security with required artifacts (build manifests, SBOMs for runtime).

Pilot ask (recommended):
- 4–6 week pilot
- Deliverables we provide: control plane installer, model pinning runbook, audit bundle, sample traffic generator, 2 SRE/SE office hours per week
- Customer deliverables: VPC & KMS access, SOC contact(s), test dataset or workload definition
- Success criteria: inferencing latency < X ms at 90p (profiled), audit log completeness verified, no data egress to public Redwood endpoints

Open questions & unresolved items (for product/security follow-up):
- Can we standardize the exact fields present in audit export to match common third-party audit tools? (Action: Product + Security)
- Is the local read-only control plane mode documented for customers who want to operate without any control plane connectivity? (Action: Docs + Eng)
- Should we offer an "allowlist-only model catalog" as an add-on in pricing tiers? (Action: GTM + Pricing)

Quick rebuttal templates (short one-liners AEs can use):
- "You keep keys — we orchestrate. Think of us as the conductor, not the vault."
- "We deliver a turnkey runtime so your infra team doesn't have to maintain kernel and batching optimizations in perpetuity."
- "If you need air-gap, we can do that — we have an installer and an airgapped onboarding checklist."

Next steps (this doc version):
- Validate with two SEs and one Security PM, incorporate technical playbook notes (target: 2024-12-10).
- Create an abridged 1-pager for AEs and a 2-slide appendix for executive briefings.

Notes to self / seller tips:
- Use simple metaphors (conductors, pinned snapshots) rather than heavy infra-speak in early buyer conversations.
- Emphasize auditability and exportability early for procurement teams.
- Keep pilot ask light and measurable — procurement teams hate open-ended pilots.

References and artifacts to attach in final version:
- Pilot runbook draft (link: CONFLUENCE-1234)
- Customer-facing DPA template
- Sample audit bundle template

End.
